prayers.title: Morning Prayer
original: God of this morning, open my ears before I speak and my hands before I grasp.
Let the work I do today be patient, honest, and useful. When I lose my way, help me begin again.
modern: God, help me listen before I speak and relax my grip on how today has to go.
Help me be honest, patient, and useful. If I forget, remind me I can start over.

prayers.title: Evening Prayer
original: God of the quiet hours, thank you for the help I received today, including the help I barely noticed.
Give me eyes to see what needs repair and the humility to rest before I try to repair it.
modern: God, thank you for the people and moments that helped me today.
Show me what I can put right. Let me rest and come back to it with a clearer mind.

prayers.title: Pause Prayer
original: God, make a little room in me between what I feel and what I do.
In that room, let me hear the wiser voice and ask for help.
modern: God, help me slow down before I act on this feeling.
Give me enough space to listen and reach out.

prayers.title: Guidance Prayer
original: God, teach me to offer my effort without demanding its reward.
Let me see the honest work in front of me and have the willingness to do it.
modern: God, help me do my part and let go of how it turns out.
Show me one honest thing I can do next, and help me do it.

prayers.title: Gratitude Prayer
original: God, turn my attention to the ordinary things that sustained me today.
May my gratitude become something I pass along, in the way I listen and in the time I make for others.
modern: God, help me notice one small thing that carried me today.
Help me pass that care along by listening or making time for someone else.

prayers.title: Prayer for a Softer Response
original: God, make me honest about what hurt and gentle about what I do with that hurt.
Help me keep the boundaries I need and release the argument I keep having in my head.
modern: God, help me name what hurt without taking it out on someone.
Help me protect what needs protecting and set down the argument I keep replaying.

prayers.title: Prayer for the Next Small Step
original: God, hold what I cannot settle today.
Give me enough courage for the task within reach and enough humility to ask someone to walk beside me.
modern: God, help me leave tomorrow alone for a minute.
Give me courage for the next small step, and help me ask someone to take it with me.

prayers.title: Prayer for Willingness
original: God, show me what I keep defending because I am afraid to change.
Give me willingness before certainty and teach me to receive correction with care.
modern: God, help me notice what I defend because change scares me.
Help me stay open to a different way, even when I feel unsure.

prayers.title: Prayer for Listening
original: God, quiet the noise I carry into this moment. Help me listen until I can hear where I’m needed.
Give me the patience to wait when the way is unclear and the courage to carry out the good I can see.
modern: God, help me slow down and listen. Show me one way I can be useful today.
Help me wait when I’m unsure and follow through when I see what to do.

prayers.title: Third Step Prayer

source.title: Alcoholics Anonymous
source.credit: Reprinted from Alcoholics Anonymous, Fourth Edition, p. 63, with permission of A.A. World Services, Inc.

original: God, I offer myself to Thee—to build with me and to do with me as Thou wilt. Relieve me of the bondage of self, that I may better do Thy will. Take away my difficulties, that victory over them may bear witness to those I would help of Thy Power, Thy Love, and Thy Way of life. May I do Thy will always!

prayers.title: Seventh Step Prayer

source.title: Alcoholics Anonymous
source.credit: Reprinted from Alcoholics Anonymous, Fourth Edition, p. 76, with permission of A.A. World Services, Inc.

original: My Creator, I am now willing that you should have all of me, good and bad. I pray that you now remove from me every single defect of character which stands in the way of my usefulness to you and my fellows. Grant me strength, as I go out from here, to do your bidding. Amen.

prayers.title: Eleventh Step Prayer

source.title: Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions
source.credit: From Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions, p. 99. Used by permission.
source.note: Peace Prayer, traditionally associated with Saint Francis of Assisi.

original: Lord, make me a channel of thy peace—that where there is hatred, I may bring love—that where there is wrong, I may bring the spirit of forgiveness—that where there is discord, I may bring harmony—that where there is error, I may bring truth—that where there is doubt, I may bring faith—that where there is despair, I may bring hope—that where there are shadows, I may bring light—that where there is sadness, I may bring joy.
Lord, grant that I may seek rather to comfort than to be comforted—to understand, than to be understood—to love, than to be loved.
For it is by self-forgetting that one finds. It is by forgiving that one is forgiven. It is by dying that one awakens to Eternal Life. Amen.

prayers.title: Upon Awakening

source.title: Alcoholics Anonymous
source.credit: Reprinted from Alcoholics Anonymous, Fourth Edition, p. 86, with permission of A.A. World Services, Inc.
source.note: The full morning guidance continues on pages 86–88.

original: On awakening let us think about the twenty-four hours ahead. We consider our plans for the day.

prayers.title: Serenity Prayer

source.title: Serenity Prayer
source.credit: Common short form, attributed to Reinhold Niebuhr.

original: God grant me the serenity to accept the things I cannot change, courage to change the things I can, and wisdom to know the difference.

prayers.title: Resentment Prayer

source.title: Alcoholics Anonymous
source.credit: Reprinted from Alcoholics Anonymous, Fourth Edition, p. 67, with permission of A.A. World Services, Inc.
source.note: This line comes from the discussion of resentment in the Fourth Step inventory.

original: God save me from being angry.

prayers.title: Fear Prayer

source.title: Alcoholics Anonymous
source.credit: Reprinted from Alcoholics Anonymous, Fourth Edition, p. 68, with permission of A.A. World Services, Inc.
source.note: The passage describes a prayer for fear in the Fourth Step inventory.

original: We ask Him to remove our fear and direct our attention to what He would have us be.

newToRecovery.title: New to Recovery
newToRecovery.intro: You can start with one meeting, one conversation, or two quiet minutes.

sections.title: Go to your first meeting
text: If you’re curious about Alcoholics Anonymous, look for an open meeting. Anyone who wants to learn about A.A. can attend. Closed meetings are for A.A. members and people who want to stop drinking. Check the listing for the time, location, and whether you can join online.

Formats vary. You may hear a reading, a speaker, or a discussion. You’re welcome to listen and share only if you want to. Afterward, you can ask the person leading the meeting which group they recommend for someone new.

links.label: What to expect at an A.A. meeting

sections.title: Ask about sponsorship
text: An A.A. sponsor is a fellow member who shares their experience and helps you work the Steps. After a meeting, ask someone you feel comfortable talking with. You can also ask the meeting chair to introduce you to someone.
sections.example: “I’m new. Would you be open to talking with me about sponsorship?”
actions: Ask what working the Steps together would look like.
Agree on how to get in touch and when to check in next.

sections.title: Take two minutes for today
text: Try this when your day begins, or whenever you need a fresh start.
actions: Pause for a few breaths.
Ask yourself what would help you stay sober today.
Pick one action you can take, such as calling someone in recovery or checking the time of a meeting.

practices.title: Morning Reflection
practices.intro: Give yourself a quiet moment before the day asks anything of you.

sections.title: Arrive
text: Feel your feet on the floor. Notice what you are bringing into the morning. Take an unhurried breath and let the day begin where you are.

sections.title: Read
text: The morning practice in the Big Book invites us to consider the day ahead and ask for help with our motives and decisions. Think of one choice you are likely to face today.

sections.title: Ask for guidance
text: Read slowly. Let one line stay with you as you move into the day.

sections.title: Choose an intention
text: Pick one place where you can be more honest, kinder, or more willing to ask for help. Picture when you will practice it.

sections.title: Carry it with you
text: If the day goes differently than you hoped, pause and begin from that moment. You can return to your intention as often as you need.

practices.title: Evening Reflection
practices.short: Look back with honesty and care.
practices.intro: Take a few minutes to look at the day with the kindness you would offer a friend.

sections.title: Settle
text: Let the day slow down. Notice your body on the chair or bed. Give yourself permission to leave some things unfinished tonight.

sections.title: Read
text: The evening review in the Big Book invites a calm look at the day, including where we owe an apology and where we could have been more helpful.

sections.title: Review gently
questions: Where did I show up for someone today?
When did fear or resentment steer my choices?
Is there something I need to tell a trusted person?

sections.title: Notice gratitude
text: Bring to mind one ordinary thing you received today: a call, a meal, a little patience, a moment outside. Let yourself notice what it gave you.

sections.title: Consider repair
text: If you owe a repair, name one thoughtful next step. Discuss it with your sponsor or a trusted peer before acting if contact could cause harm.

sections.title: Close the day
text: Read the prayer, or use a few words of your own. Give yourself a chance to rest.

situations.title: I’m feeling resentful
situations.grounding: It can take a lot of energy to replay something that hurt. Give yourself a few quiet minutes before you decide what to do.
situations.principle: Honesty and perspective. Name the harm and notice what is yours to handle today. Keeping a boundary can be part of that.
actions: Set aside the reply you are composing, if it can safely wait.
Describe what happened in one sentence. Then name the feeling it brought up.
Ask yourself what would help you respond in a way you can live with tomorrow.
situations.connection: Talk it through with your sponsor or a trusted peer before reacting. Ask them to help you sort a useful boundary from the urge to get even.

situations.title: I’m afraid or anxious
situations.grounding: You can feel afraid and still take one small step. Start by noticing one thing you can see and the support beneath your feet.
situations.principle: Courage. Name the fear, then look for one action within reach.
actions: Name the specific outcome you are afraid of.
Separate what you know from what you are imagining.
Choose one step you can take in the next ten minutes.
situations.connection: Tell someone you trust exactly what you are afraid might happen. Ask them to stay with you while you decide what to do.

situations.title: I’m struggling with an urge to drink or use
situations.grounding: Call someone you trust now. Move somewhere safer if you can.
situations.principle: Connection. Say plainly what is happening and let someone help you through the next few minutes.
actions: Call your sponsor, a trusted person, or a recovery peer. Say “I’m having an urge and I need someone with me.”
If the first person is unavailable, try the next person or use a crisis line for live support.
Ask a sober person to help you get somewhere safer or stay with you. If you have used, avoid driving.
situations.connection: Read or pray while you wait for a reply if that helps. Keep reaching for live support.
situations.detailTitle: An urge to drink or use

situations.title: I’m angry or frustrated
situations.grounding: Give the anger a little room. Try uncurling your hands or taking a step away from the conversation if that is safe.
situations.principle: Restraint. Delay a reply long enough to hear what the anger is asking for.
actions: Put your phone down and take a short break from the exchange.
Name what you need in plain language, such as space, respect, or clarity.
When you are ready, ask directly for what you need.
situations.connection: Call someone who can listen and help you decide when it is safe and useful to return to the conversation.

situations.title: I’m overwhelmed
situations.grounding: Put one task down and let the next minute be small. A sip of water or a seat can be a starting point.
situations.principle: Simplicity. Give your attention to what needs care first.
actions: Name the one thing that genuinely needs attention now.
Pick something that can wait until tomorrow.
Ask for help with one task instead of carrying it by yourself.
situations.connection: Text someone a simple request, like “Could I talk for a few minutes while I figure out what needs doing first?”

situations.title: I’m feeling lonely
situations.grounding: Feeling far from other people can hurt. A small point of contact is enough to begin.
situations.principle: Fellowship. Let someone hear your voice, or make room to hear theirs.
actions: Send a short hello to someone from a meeting.
Consider a meeting, a walk with a friend, or a call to a trusted person.
If speaking feels hard, ask someone if you can just listen for a while.
situations.connection: Try saying “I could use some company today.” You can share as much as you feel ready to share.

situations.title: I’m struggling with guilt or shame
situations.grounding: Give yourself time to tell the truth kindly. Start with what happened and how it affected you or someone else.
situations.principle: Accountability with compassion. You can face a mistake and still deserve help.
actions: Name the action that troubles you in one factual sentence.
Ask what responsibility is yours and what support you need.
Wait to contact anyone you may have harmed until you have talked through the consequences.
situations.connection: Ask a safe, trusted person to listen. If you feel at risk of harming yourself, reach emergency or crisis support now.

situations.title: I’m having trouble accepting something
situations.grounding: Some things take time to accept. Start by naming what is already true today.
situations.principle: Acceptance. Face the facts and use your energy where you still have a choice.
actions: Describe what has already happened in plain terms.
Choose one part of your response you can influence.
Give yourself permission to grieve or feel angry while you take that step.
situations.connection: Ask your sponsor or a trusted peer what they hear when you describe the situation. They may see an option you are too close to notice.

situations.title: I need to make a difficult decision
situations.grounding: If you have time, give the decision some breathing room. A pause can make it easier to hear your own judgment.
situations.principle: Willingness. Ask for direction and consider who might be affected by the choice.
actions: Identify the decision and when it actually needs to be made.
Name the choice that fits your values, even if it is uncomfortable.
Review your options with someone who can listen without deciding for you.
situations.connection: Ask a sponsor or trusted person to help you think through your motives and the likely effects of each choice.

situations.title: I just need some perspective
situations.grounding: Step back from the part of the day that is taking up all the room. There may be more to the picture.
situations.principle: Gratitude. Notice what is steady, what is changing, and where you can be useful.
actions: Describe what is happening as if you were telling a friend.
Notice one person, place, or practice that has helped you lately.
Choose one small thing you can do to care for yourself or someone else.
situations.connection: Ask someone you trust how they have handled a similar day. Listen for one thing you could try.

steps.title: Honesty about alcohol
steps.intro: Look at what happens once drinking begins and how it has affected your life. Honest examples can help you decide what support you need now.
questions: Where did I try to manage drinking on my own?
What happened when I made rules about when or how much I could drink?
exercises: Work through one recent episode with your sponsor. Begin before the first drink and follow through to the next day. Notice where asking for help might fit.

steps.title: Opening to help
steps.intro: Explore where help might come from beyond your own familiar efforts. A group, a spiritual understanding, or the example of people in recovery may give you a place to begin.
questions: Whose recovery gives me reason to hope?
What kind of help could I become willing to accept?
exercises: Choose a person whose recovery you respect and ask what helped them stay open early on.

steps.title: Choosing a direction
steps.intro: Make a decision to seek guidance in how you live. Discuss what turning over a decision means in practice and how you will follow it with action.
questions: Where am I trying to control an outcome I cannot control?
What does a decision to seek guidance look like in my own language?
exercises: Choose one decision to discuss with a sponsor. Name the part you can do, then practice letting other people make their own choices.

steps.title: Taking inventory
steps.intro: A structured inventory can reveal recurring resentments, fears, and conduct patterns. Work at a pace agreed with your sponsor and keep your written notes somewhere private.
questions: What am I hesitant to put into words?
What patterns show up across different people or situations?
Where do I need to distinguish harm done to me from actions I can take responsibility for?
exercises: Agree on a manageable amount before you begin. Try one resentment, one fear, and one relationship example. Look for a repeating response or need, then discuss it with your sponsor.

steps.title: Sharing the inventory
steps.intro: Speak honestly about what you discovered with a carefully chosen person. Agree on privacy, time, and breaks before you share.
questions: Who can listen with care and keep a confidence?
What feels hardest to say out loud?
exercises: Set aside an unhurried time. Talk about confidentiality and boundaries before beginning. Ask for a break if you need one.

steps.title: Becoming ready
steps.intro: Notice the habits you still lean on when you feel threatened, and consider what it would take to let those habits change.
questions: What familiar behavior still feels protective?
What would willingness look like before I feel ready?
exercises: Pick one recurring behavior. Talk through what it does for you and name a different response you could practice this week.

steps.title: Asking for change
steps.intro: Ask for help with a shortcoming that keeps hurting you or others. Give that request shape by practicing a different action in a familiar situation.
questions: What change am I willing to ask for today?
Who sees this pattern clearly enough to give me honest feedback?
exercises: Before a situation where the pattern usually appears, ask for help and choose one alternative action. Check in afterward.

steps.title: Preparing for repair
steps.intro: Identify the people affected by your actions. Consider the harm with care, then talk through possible repairs before making contact.
questions: Who felt the effects of what I did?
Where do I feel willing to make repair, and where do I feel stuck?
exercises: Make a private list on paper and review it with a sponsor. Identify practical repair, safety concerns, and cases that need more guidance.

steps.title: Making amends
steps.intro: Take responsibility in ways that serve the person affected. Think through timing, safety, and consequences with your sponsor before approaching anyone.
questions: What repair would be useful to the other person?
Could direct contact cause harm or disregard someone’s boundaries?
exercises: Rehearse one amends with your sponsor. Include the action and possible repair. Respect a person’s choice to decline contact.

steps.title: Checking in as you go
steps.intro: Pay attention when an old response appears. When you have done harm, acknowledge it and act on what can be put right.
questions: What repeated itself today?
What can I acknowledge or repair promptly?
exercises: Try a brief pause after a tense interaction. Name what happened, ask for help if needed, and consider a reasonable repair.

steps.title: Making time for guidance
steps.intro: Set aside a little space for prayer, meditation, or quiet reflection. Try a practice you can return to in daily life.
questions: When is it easiest to get quiet?
What helps me listen before acting on a decision?
exercises: Try the morning or evening reflection for a few days. Discuss with your sponsor where the practice helped you notice a choice.

steps.title: Carrying recovery forward
steps.intro: Share your own recovery experience when it is welcome, and look for places to practice the principles in ordinary relationships.
questions: What service am I able to offer consistently?
Where can I practice the principles away from meetings?
exercises: Choose one manageable act of service. Ask what is actually needed and follow through on what you offer.

readings.title: More About Alcoholism
readings.instructions: Read for examples of returning to a drink after promising to stop. Bring one passage and one experience of your own to discuss.
questions: Where did I try to manage drinking on my own?
What happened when I made rules about when or how much I could drink?

readings.title: We Agnostics
readings.instructions: Read at your own pace. Mark places that invite you to consider a different possibility, including places you disagree with.
questions: Whose recovery gives me reason to hope?
What kind of help could I become willing to accept?

readings.title: Step 3 reading
readings.instructions: Read the lead-in to the Third Step Prayer. Think about how the decision could show up in one ordinary responsibility.
questions: Where am I trying to control an outcome I cannot control?
What does a decision to seek guidance look like in my own language?

readings.title: Step 4 reading
readings.instructions: Read the inventory examples before choosing a format. Notice where the text moves from describing events to examining repeated responses.
questions: What am I hesitant to put into words?
What patterns show up across different people or situations?
Where do I need to distinguish harm done to me from actions I can take responsibility for?

readings.title: Step 5 reading
readings.instructions: Read the discussion of choosing a listener and preparing to speak candidly. Identify what would help you feel able to be truthful.
questions: Who can listen with care and keep a confidence?
What feels hardest to say out loud?

readings.title: Step 6 reading
readings.instructions: Read the transition from sharing inventory to asking for change. Think about a pattern you have defended and what it has cost.
questions: What familiar behavior still feels protective?
What would willingness look like before I feel ready?

readings.title: Step 7 reading
readings.instructions: Read the Seventh Step passage. Discuss what it means to be useful while still learning.
questions: What change am I willing to ask for today?
Who sees this pattern clearly enough to give me honest feedback?

readings.title: Step 8 reading
readings.instructions: Read the transition into amends. Consider where your inventory already names damage you can acknowledge.
questions: Who felt the effects of what I did?
Where do I feel willing to make repair, and where do I feel stuck?

readings.title: Step 9 reading
readings.instructions: Read the examples of different kinds of amends. Discuss what the repair serves and who might be affected by contact.
questions: What repair would be useful to the other person?
Could direct contact cause harm or disregard someone’s boundaries?

readings.title: Step 10 reading
readings.instructions: Read the daily inventory passage. Look for the sequence from noticing a reaction to discussing it and turning toward a useful action.
questions: What repeated itself today?
What can I acknowledge or repair promptly?

readings.title: Step 11 reading
readings.instructions: Read the guidance for the beginning and end of the day. Choose one practice to try at a time that fits your life.
questions: When is it easiest to get quiet?
What helps me listen before acting on a decision?

readings.title: Working With Others
readings.instructions: Read for ways to offer help while respecting another person’s decisions. Notice what the chapter suggests about listening and sharing experience.
questions: What service am I able to offer consistently?
Where can I practice the principles away from meetings?

readings.title: A review at day’s end
readings.instructions: Read the evening review slowly. Choose one question about the day and sit with it before considering any response.
questions: Where did I offer or receive help today?
What would be useful to put right tomorrow?

worksheets.title: Resentment inventory
worksheets.intro: Use one sheet for one situation. Start with facts, then explore the feelings and responses. If someone harmed you, take care to distinguish their actions from your own.
fields: Who or what am I resentful toward?
Name the person, situation, or institution.
What happened?
Describe the event in plain terms.
What felt affected?
Consider security, self-respect, relationships, or plans.
How did I respond?
Notice patterns, boundaries, and choices within your control.
What can I discuss with my sponsor?
Name one question or next action.

worksheets.title: Fear inventory
worksheets.intro: Begin with a specific fear you are comfortable exploring. Discuss the format and pace with your sponsor.
fields: What am I afraid of?
Name the outcome you fear.
What brings this fear up?
Consider facts, memories, and assumptions.
What do I do when I feel it?
Look for avoidance, control, or attempts to handle it alone.
Where could I seek help?
Name a person, a spiritual practice, or a practical next step.

worksheets.title: Sex and conduct inventory
worksheets.intro: Review conduct in a relationship or encounter at a pace you choose. Focus on your choices. A violation or abuse by someone else is their responsibility.
fields: What was the situation?
Use as much detail as you need to understand your own conduct.
How did I act?
Consider honesty, consent, boundaries, and care.
Who was affected and how?
Think about consequences without guessing at another person’s feelings.
How would I like to act today?
Name a boundary, value, or behavior you want to practice.
What needs discussion before action?
Consult your sponsor and appropriate support before attempting a repair.

worksheets.title: Evening check-in
worksheets.intro: Use this page privately if writing helps you reflect. Answer only the questions that are useful today.
fields: What went well?
Name an action you appreciate or help you received.
What needs attention?
Notice a reaction, a worry, or a conversation you need to have.
What can I do next?
Choose a reasonable repair or a person to talk with.

resources.title: Your first sponsorship conversation
resources.intro: Agree on what you each need and can offer.

sections.title: Before you meet
items: Ask how and when you can reach each other.
Talk about meeting frequency and how you prefer to read or discuss assignments.
Agree on privacy and what to do if either of you needs a different arrangement.

sections.title: Before you leave
text: Choose one realistic next step and a time to check in. Keep urgent support options available alongside your regular contact plan.

resources.title: A practical sponsor check-in
resources.intro: A short guide for making the most of a conversation.

sections.title: Begin with what matters today
items: What feels most important to talk about right now?
What did you learn from the assignment or practice?
Where did you ask for help, or where could you try asking?

sections.title: Agree on a next step
text: Reflect back what you heard. Invite the other person to choose a specific action and decide when to follow up.

resources.title: Sponsorship with care and boundaries
resources.intro: Share experience, respect autonomy, and make room for other support.

sections.title: Share from experience
text: Describe what helped you and invite questions. People work the Steps in different ways. Make room for someone to ask for another viewpoint.

sections.title: Keep clear boundaries
items: Agree on availability and confidentiality and revisit them when circumstances change.
Encourage a wider network of peers and appropriate professional care.
Respect each person’s decisions, relationships, and spiritual language.

toolkitGroups.title: Working the Twelve Steps
toolkitGroups.description: Find a guide for each step.

toolkitGroups.title: Reading Assignments
toolkitGroups.description: Literature references to share and discuss.

toolkitGroups.title: Sponsorship Principles
toolkitGroups.description: Share experience with care and respect.

topics.title: Progress, Not Perfection
topics.opening: What does making progress actually look like when life is messy?
questions: Where has perfectionism gotten in your way?
What small change are you proud of?
How do you respond when you fall short?

topics.title: The First Step
topics.label: Step 1
topics.opening: What changed when you became willing to acknowledge powerlessness?
questions: What did trying to control drinking look like?
What does unmanageability mean to you today?
How has acceptance changed your choices?

topics.title: Hope Before Certainty
topics.label: Step 2
topics.opening: What helped you stay when you were not sure recovery could work?
questions: Who gave you hope early on?
Can willingness come before belief?
What would you tell someone at their first meeting?

topics.title: Turning It Over
topics.label: Step 3
topics.opening: How do you practice letting go without giving up responsibility?
questions: What are you still trying to control?
What action is yours to take today?
How do you recognize when you need help?

topics.title: Honest Self-Inventory
topics.label: Step 4
topics.opening: What have you learned from looking at your own patterns?
questions: What is the difference between guilt and accountability?
Which pattern surprised you?
How can you be thorough without being cruel to yourself?

topics.title: The Courage to Share
topics.label: Step 5
topics.opening: What changes when we stop carrying our story alone?
questions: What made it hard to be honest?
What did being heard mean to you?
Where does secrecy still show up?

topics.title: Becoming Ready
topics.label: Step 6
topics.opening: What does willingness to change look like in practice?
questions: Which habit are you most attached to?
Can you want change and fear it at the same time?
What helps you become more willing?

topics.title: Humility in Action
topics.label: Step 7
topics.opening: How is humility different from thinking less of yourself?
questions: When is asking for help an act of strength?
Where do you confuse humility with shame?
What does a humble action look like today?

topics.title: The Amends List
topics.label: Step 8
topics.opening: How do you face past harm without getting stuck in regret?
questions: What makes someone difficult to put on a list?
How is willingness different from readiness?
Where is guidance important?

topics.title: Making Things Right
topics.label: Step 9
topics.opening: What makes an amends meaningful beyond saying sorry?
questions: How is an amends different from an apology?
Why does timing matter?
How do you respect another person’s boundaries?

topics.title: A Daily Course Correction
topics.label: Step 10
topics.opening: How can we recognize mistakes and address them promptly?
questions: How do you notice resentment building?
What gets in the way of admitting a mistake?
What helps you correct course quickly?

topics.title: Quiet Time
topics.label: Step 11
topics.opening: How do prayer or meditation fit into your daily life?
questions: What makes quiet time difficult?
When have you benefited from pausing?
What is one small routine you can keep?

topics.title: Carrying the Message
topics.label: Step 12
topics.opening: What does being useful to another person look like?
questions: What did someone do for you when you arrived?
Where is listening more helpful than advising?
How can service stay simple?

topics.title: One Day at a Time
topics.opening: How does focusing on today change the way you face recovery?
questions: What happens when you project too far ahead?
What is enough for today?
How do you get through a difficult hour?
